plan.topic: How science cracked plague: finding Yersinia pestis (Hong Kong, 1894), proving the flea route (1898–1914), and the 1910–11 pneumonic plague outbreak in Manchuria, where masks, isolation and contact tracing first showed what stops person-to-person spread
plan.angle: Plague History: How Scientists Found the Cause and Learned to Stop It. Open with the dated suspected-status hook (15 s or less; newest development first; includes the Oct 8 Tedros and Kremlin entries and the Oct 9 Irkutsk oblast governor update; not ending on the most reassuring line; re-checked at publish time). Body: (1) Hong Kong 1894: Alexandre Yersin isolated the bacterium, later named Yersinia pestis; Kitasato Shibasaburo also studied it there, and credit was disputed. (2) Paul-Louis Simond proposed the rat-flea route in 1898, and Bacot and Martin's 1914 'blocked flea' work explained how fleas pass it on. (3) Manchuria 1910–11, a pneumonic outbreak: Wu Lien-teh's response (gauze masks, isolation, contact tracing, travel controls) showed at scale how to stop close-contact spread; deaths given as an estimate with the source's range; quarantine itself is centuries older. (4) What modern public health took from it, in CDC's wording: droplet spread that typically 'requires direct and close contact'; 'can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early'; spread 'has not been documented in the United States since 1924'. Close with CDC's 4 pneumonic signs (fever, cough, shortness of breath, chest pain); possible exposure means contact a doctor or local health authority urgently; 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'
plan.working_title: Plague History: How Scientists Found the Cause and Learned to Stop It
plan.trend_stage: evergreen (refreshed with a timely news hook)
plan.why:
Replaces dropped L1 and L2 with a well-documented history explainer that fact-checks easily, needs only one dated status hedge, and doesn't repeat the Black Death carousel, Madagascar, lab safety or today's Shorts and carousel. | fact-check: Approve the history-of-science angle. It's evergreen, built on settled sources, calm, and serves the plague focus without doom framing. Five accuracy fixes before scripting:
(1) The topic line overclaims. Isolation and quarantine are centuries older than 1910: plague quarantine dates to 14th–15th-century Ragusa and Venice. So Manchuria didn't 'first show' them. Say Wu Lien-teh's response showed at scale, in a pneumonic outbreak, that masks, isolation, tracing and travel controls could stop person-to-person spread. Don't call his gauze mask the first mask. Say it was an early, influential use of masks against a respiratory epidemic.
(2) 1894 discovery: Kitasato Shibasaburo also worked on the bacterium in Hong Kong in 1894, and credit was disputed. Mention him in one neutral line, saying Yersin's description is the one credited today. Yersin isolated it and the name Yersinia pestis came decades later (it was earlier called Pasteurella pestis). Keep 'later named' and don't give a renaming year unless a source states it.
(3) Simond 1898: he proposed the rat-flea route based on observations and small experiments, and it wasn't widely accepted at first. Say 'proposed', not 'proved'. 1898–1914 is fine as the period when the flea route was worked out. Bacot and Martin's 1914 blocked-flea paper explains the mechanism.
(4) Manchuria death toll: label it as an estimate and give the source's figure and range (often cited as about 60,000). Don't present a single figure as fact.
(5) Black Death comparison: don't say how much of the Black Death was bubonic and how much pneumonic, because historians still debate it. Limit the 'why today is different' point to what CDC and WHO say: antibiotics and public-health measures.
CDC wording to copy exactly: pneumonic plague is the only form that can spread person to person, through infectious respiratory droplets, and typically 'requires direct and close contact'. Plague 'can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early'. Spread 'has not been documented in the United States since 1924'. Never write '1924 was the last spread'. The status block and its dates (Oct 8 Tedros and Kremlin, Oct 9 governor) must be re-checked at publish time and checked again in content_check. Keep the status within the 15 s hook, using 'suspected'/'reported', and never end on the most reassuring line. No drug names, doses or test terms. Title: fine as is, starts with 'Plague', no abbreviations, no fear words.

script.working_title: Plague History: How Scientists Found the Cause and Learned to Stop It
script.hook_pattern: Dated status hook, newest development first. As of Oct 10, 2026, plague is 'reported as suspected, but not confirmed'. Next come the Oct 8 governor and Rospotrebnadzor entries, then the Oct 7 Kremlin/Tedros entries. The status ends on the open WHO question, not on the most reassuring line, and all dates get re-checked against the WHO briefing transcript at publish time. Then an open loop: 'the one rule from 1911 that still decides who gets watched after a suspected case'. It pays off in 'What we still use'.

scenes.narration: As of Oct 10, 2026, plague has been reported as suspected, but not confirmed, in a laboratory worker in Irkutsk oblast who died. On Oct 6, WHO said authorities were looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death. Rospotrebnadzor describes it as pneumonia of unknown origin.
scenes.on_screen_text: Reported as suspected, NOT CONFIRMED (as of Oct 10, 2026)
scenes.retention_device: The newest dated status comes first, so viewers get the news answer within seconds

scenes.narration: Newest, on Oct 8: the Irkutsk oblast governor said about 5,000 lab tests found no dangerous pathogens, that medical monitoring of all contacts had ended, and that she had community-acquired pneumonia. AP noted he did not explicitly say whether pneumonic plague had been ruled out.
scenes.on_screen_text: Oct 8: governor: ~5,000 tests, contact monitoring ended

visual.stat_label: lab tests, per Irkutsk oblast governor (Oct 8)
visual.stock_query: rows of lab test tubes cartoon

scenes.retention_device: A concrete number in the opening beat

scenes.narration: Also on Oct 8, Rospotrebnadzor said it had told WHO no case of plague has been registered in the Irkutsk region, and rejected reports of a second person falling ill. A day earlier, on Oct 7, the Kremlin called most media reports false, and WHO chief Tedros asked Russia to clarify media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause.

Oct 7: Kremlin calls most media reports false
Oct 7: WHO's Tedros asks about a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause

scenes.retention_device: The status ends on the open WHO question, not on the most reassuring line

scenes.narration: We'll keep updating that, with dates. But here's something that isn't in doubt. Health agencies have a playbook for stopping plague spreading between people, and it was written more than a century ago.

visual.stock_query: old notebook glowing on modern desk

scenes.retention_device: Pattern interrupt: a pivot from the news to a century-old mystery

scenes.narration: It took three breakthroughs. A scientist in a straw hut in Hong Kong. A doctor with two rats and a jar. And a 31-year-old physician with a strip of gauze.

items: Karachi, 1898: two rats and a jar

scenes.retention_device: Promises a three-part story with vivid teasers

scenes.narration: By the end, you'll know the one rule from 1911 that still decides who gets watched after a suspected case, and why it works.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop, paid off in 'What we still use'

scenes.narration: Spring, 1894. Plague, already spreading in southern China, reaches Hong Kong, one of the busiest ports on Earth.
Historians count this as the start of the third plague pandemic. Ships would carry it to ports around the world.
And nobody knew what caused it. Germ theory was still young, and the race to find the culprit was on.
Two scientists arrived that June. Kitasato Shibasaburo, a Japanese bacteriologist who had trained with Robert Koch. And Alexandre Yersin, a Swiss-born doctor from France's Pasteur Institute.
Kitasato's team had hospital access. Yersin, by the usual telling, set up in a makeshift straw hut.
scenes.on_screen_text: A lab in a straw hut

scenes.narration: He took samples from the swollen lymph nodes, called buboes, of people who had died. Under the microscope: crowds of the same short, rod-shaped bacterium.
He found the same bacterium in dead rats from the streets. A clue, though not yet an answer.

visual.stock_query: detective magnifying glass over rat silhouette

scenes.narration: One often-told detail: without a proper incubator, he grew his cultures at room temperature. And this bacterium happens to grow well below body temperature.
He gave the bacteria to lab animals, they fell ill, and the same germ turned up in them. That's the chain of evidence that ties one germ to one disease.
Kitasato also reported a bacterium that summer, and for decades credit was disputed. Today, Yersin's description is the one credited.
For decades the germ was known as Pasteurella pestis. It was later renamed Yersinia pestis, after him.

visual.stock_query: name label swapped on specimen jar

scenes.narration: But naming the killer didn't explain the crime. How was it getting from rats into people? That answer took 20 years, and it starts with an insect about the size of a sesame seed.

visual.stock_query: tiny flea next to sesame seed

scenes.narration: Karachi, 1898. Paul-Louis Simond, a French doctor working for the Pasteur Institute, is studying plague in what was then British India.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card and a new character

scenes.narration: He noticed patterns. Some patients had a tiny blister on the skin, like a bite mark. And some people fell ill after handling dead rats.
scenes.on_screen_text: A tiny blister, like a bite

scenes.narration: His idea: fleas leave a dying rat looking for a new host. Maybe, sometimes, that host is us.
scenes.on_screen_text: Fleas looking for a new host

scenes.narration: So he built a test. A sick rat at the bottom of a jar. A healthy rat in a small cage above it, kept apart so they couldn't touch. Only fleas could make the jump.

visual.stock_query: glass jar two cartoon rats cage

scenes.narration: Days later, the healthy rat had plague.
He later wrote that he felt an inexpressible emotion, believing he'd uncovered a secret that had troubled humanity since plague first appeared.
scenes.on_screen_text: A secret as old as plague

visual.stock_query: scientist moved by discovery at desk

scenes.narration: But here's the twist: hardly anyone believed him. His experiments were small, and others couldn't always reproduce them. He had proposed the flea route; he hadn't proved it.

visual.myth: Simond proved fleas spread plague in 1898
visual.fact: He proposed it; larger studies backed it later

scenes.narration: Over the following decade, larger experiments in India by a plague research commission backed the flea route.

visual.stock_query: team of scientists with many jars

scenes.narration: Yet one puzzle remained. Most insect bites don't give you plague. So what made these fleas so good at spreading it?
scenes.retention_device: A question to the viewer that opens a new loop

scenes.narration: In 1914, two researchers in London, Arthur Bacot and Charles Martin, watched infected fleas up close.
In some fleas, the bacteria grew into a sticky mass that blocked the passage into the flea's stomach.
So the flea starves. It bites again and again, trying to feed. And each time, blood gets pushed back out into the bite, carrying bacteria with it.
Picture a clogged sink. Pour water in, and it backs up. Here, what backs up carries the germ.
Modern research suggests fleas can also pass plague on before they're fully blocked, and scientists still study how much each route matters.
By 1914, the classic chain was mapped. Rodents carry it. Fleas move it. A bite passes it to people.

items: A bite passes it to people

scenes.narration: CDC says people most often get plague from infected flea bites, and also by handling tissue or body fluids of an infected animal.
scenes.on_screen_text: Flea bites, or handling infected animals

scenes.narration: But there's one form of plague that doesn't need a flea at all. And in the winter of 1910, it broke out along a railway in Manchuria.
Late 1910. Plague appears in Manchuria, in northeast China, starting near the Russian border and spreading along the railway.
Many early cases were linked to hunters of marmots, wild rodents trapped for their fur.
But this outbreak was different. Patients developed pneumonia and died within days. This was pneumonic plague, infection in the lungs.
And with no antibiotics yet, nearly everyone who caught it died.
The Qing government sent a young doctor to Harbin: Wu Lien-teh. Born in Penang, trained at Cambridge, and just 31 years old.

Wu examined the body of a patient who had died and found plague bacteria in the lungs. His conclusion: this outbreak was passing from person to person through the breath, not mainly through rats and fleas.
scenes.on_screen_text: Person to person, not mainly fleas

scenes.narration: Then he did something almost absurdly simple. He designed a mask: layers of gauze around a pad of cotton, tied behind the head.
To be clear, it wasn't the first mask ever. But it was an early, influential use of masks against a respiratory epidemic.

visual.myth: Wu invented the first face mask
visual.fact: An early, influential mask against a respiratory epidemic

scenes.narration: Not everyone was convinced. A senior French doctor in Harbin, Gérald Mesny, reportedly doubted Wu and went without a mask. Within days, he caught plague and died.
scenes.retention_device: A dramatic turning point told as a micro-story

scenes.narration: After that, masks spread fast among doctors, nurses and the public.
But here's what most people miss. The mask was only one piece. The real power came from four measures working together.
Sick people were isolated in plague hospitals. Their contacts were tracked down and quarantined, some in railway carriages turned into observation wards.
Inspection teams went house to house looking for new cases. And travel on the railway was restricted, so the infection couldn't ride the trains.
Historians credit these measures with helping end it. By the spring of 1911, the epidemic was over.
The toll was still enormous: commonly estimated at about 60,000 deaths, though figures vary between sources.
scenes.retention_device: A sobering stat with an honest hedge

scenes.narration: That April, Wu chaired an International Plague Conference in Mukden, where scientists from many countries compared what they'd learned.
Now, one important caveat. Quarantine wasn't invented in Manchuria. It was first introduced in 1377 in Dubrovnik, then the port of Ragusa, on Croatia's coast.
Isolation periods of 40 days, quaranta giorni in Italian, became the standard, and gave us the word quarantine.
So what Manchuria showed was something specific. At scale, in a pneumonic outbreak, masks, isolation, contact tracing and travel controls together could stop person-to-person spread.
And that brings us back to the rule I promised you.
scenes.retention_device: Signals the payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: Here it is. Pneumonic plague spreads between people through close contact. So you don't screen everyone. You find the people who were close, and you watch them.
CDC says pneumonic plague is the only form that can spread from person to person, through infectious droplets. And that requires direct and close contact.
scenes.on_screen_text: Only pneumonic spreads person to person
scenes.retention_device: The agency's own wording on screen

scenes.narration: That's the logic behind watching close contacts after a suspected case. Same idea as Wu's, just with better tools.
scenes.retention_device: Links the past to the present

scenes.narration: The biggest new tool is one Wu never had: antibiotics. CDC says plague can be cured with antibiotics, but they must be given promptly.

WHO's guidance includes tracing close contacts of pneumonic plague patients and offering them preventive antibiotics. That's a decision for health authorities and clinicians, never something to do on your own.

visual.stock_query: public health team planning at table

scenes.narration: Here's a calming fact, in CDC's own words: person-to-person spread has not been documented in the United States since 1924.
scenes.on_screen_text: Not documented in the US since 1924

visual.stat_label: person-to-person spread not documented since (US, CDC)

scenes.retention_device: A surprising, reassuring stat in the agency's exact wording

scenes.narration: Plague hasn't vanished, though. It still circulates in small mammals and their fleas. WHO says that from 2019 to 2025, most cases reported to it were in DR Congo and Madagascar.
So what really separates today from the Black Death? It isn't luck. It's antibiotics, plus public health systems that find cases and cut off spread.
Which leaves one practical question: what should you actually watch for?
scenes.retention_device: A question to the viewer before the final chapter

scenes.narration: Signs CDC lists for pneumonic plague include fever, cough, shortness of breath and chest pain.

If you might have been exposed, for example through close contact with someone with suspected pneumonic plague, or by handling tissue or body fluids of an infected animal, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently.
scenes.on_screen_text: Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently

scenes.narration: Tell them about the possible exposure and any travel. Don't self-treat, and don't stockpile antibiotics. Testing and treatment decisions belong with clinicians.
And if you're worried, talk to a health professional.

So, the century-long detective story in four lines. 1894: the germ is found. 1898 to 1914: the flea route is worked out. 1910 to 1911: close-contact spread is stopped at scale. Today: antibiotics plus contact tracing.

Official statements about the Irkutsk oblast case are still coming in. Subscribe to InforMed and you'll get each update dated, sourced and calm, as soon as we've checked what health agencies have said.
scenes.retention_device: CTA tied to a specific next benefit

factcheck.summary:
The history sections hold up well. Simond, Bacot and Martin, Wu, Mesny, the about 60,000 deaths, Mukden 1911 and Ragusa 1377 all match standard sources, and the Wu facts are confirmed in the Protein & Cell article. The CDC and WHO claims also match the current pages: How Plague Spreads (updated May 15, 2024), About Plague (Aug 24, 2026), Signs and Symptoms (May 15, 2024) and the WHO fact sheet (Sep 29, 2026). The safety lines are there: the urgent-contact line, no self-treatment, and "If you're worried, talk to a health professional."

The status dates are correct. Al Jazeera says Peskov and Tedros spoke "on Wednesday" (Oct 7). AP says Kobzev and Rospotrebnadzor spoke "Thursday" (Oct 8).

Two attribution problems in the news beats need fixing before publish:
- s03 credits Rospotrebnadzor with telling WHO that no plague case was registered. Neither cited source says this. In reporting, that line is Tedros relaying what "Russian health authorities" told WHO, and it includes the word "recently".
- s01 credits "pneumonia of unknown origin" to Rospotrebnadzor and paraphrases WHO's Oct 6 statement more loosely than the cited UN News text.

There are also a few minor wording fixes.

issues.claim: Also on Oct 8, Rospotrebnadzor said it had told WHO no case of plague has been registered in the Irkutsk region
issues.problem: Neither cited source (AP/KSAT, Al Jazeera) says this. AP only says that 'earlier Thursday, Rospotrebnadzor rejected reports about a second person falling ill'. In other coverage, the 'no case of plague had recently been registered in Irkutsk region' line comes from WHO's Tedros, relaying what Russian health authorities told WHO. So this credits the claim to the wrong body and drops 'recently', which is the same kind of mistake that caused earlier holds.
issues.fix: Narration: "Also on Oct 8, Rospotrebnadzor rejected reports of a second person falling ill, AP reports. A day earlier, on Oct 7, the Kremlin called most media reports false, and WHO chief Tedros asked Russia to clarify media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause." List item 1: "Oct 8: Rospotrebnadzor rejects reports of a second person falling ill (AP)"

issues.claim: On Oct 6, WHO said authorities were looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death. Rospotrebnadzor describes it as pneumonia of unknown origin.
issues.problem: The cited UN News piece (Oct 6) quotes WHO's Christian Lindmeier: 'No cause of death has been officially confirmed to date and laboratory testing is reportedly underway.' Our narration paraphrases this more loosely. None of the cited sources credits 'pneumonia of unknown origin' to Rospotrebnadzor. Al Jazeera credits 'pneumonia of unknown aetiology' to Russia generally, and that wording came before the governor's Oct 8 'community-acquired pneumonia', so the present tense 'describes' is out of date.
issues.fix: "As of Oct 10, 2026, plague has been reported as suspected, but not confirmed, in a laboratory worker in Irkutsk oblast who died. Russian authorities said she had pneumonia of unknown aetiology. On Oct 6, WHO said no cause of death had been officially confirmed and laboratory testing was reportedly underway."

issues.claim: Oct 8: governor: ~5,000 tests, contact monitoring ended
issues.problem: The card drops AP's caveat that he did not explicitly say whether pneumonic plague had been ruled out. On its own it reads as an all-clear. On-screen text should never be more reassuring than the narration.
issues.fix: "Oct 8, governor: ~5,000 tests, monitoring ended. Plague NOT RULED OUT explicitly (AP)"

issues.claim: CDC says plague can be cured with antibiotics, but they must be given promptly.
issues.problem: CDC's About Plague page (updated Aug 24, 2026) says 'Plague can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment must be given quickly.' Because we credit the line to CDC on screen, we should use CDC's exact words.
issues.fix: Narration: "CDC says plague can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment must be given quickly." On-screen: "Curable with antibiotics; treatment must be given quickly (CDC)"

issues.claim: WHO's guidance includes tracing close contacts of pneumonic plague patients and offering them preventive antibiotics.
issues.problem: This is accurate but less precise than the source. The WHO fact sheet (updated Sep 29, 2026) says 'Identify and monitor close contacts of pneumonic plague patients and give them a seven-day chemoprophylaxis.'
issues.fix: "WHO's guidance is to identify and monitor close contacts of pneumonic plague patients and give them preventive antibiotics. That's a decision for health authorities and clinicians, never something to do on your own."

issues.claim: Isolation periods of 40 days ... became the standard
issues.problem: Tognotti says the 1377 Ragusa rule set a 30-day isolation ('trentino'), which was later extended to 40 days. Without that, viewers may assume 40 days applied from 1377.
issues.fix: "Ragusa's first rule was 30 days. It was later extended to 40, quaranta giorni in Italian, which gave us the word quarantine."
